content: Tubal sterilization via hysteroscopy involves the insertion of a foreign body into both fallopian tubes. Over a period of three months, tissue growth stimulated by the inserted device leads to occlusion of the tubal lumen. This method offers certain advantages over laparoscopic or mini-laparotomy sterilization, such as avoiding abdominal incisions and allowing the procedure to be performed in an office-based setting. However, pain management is a critical factor in determining the acceptability of this procedure, particularly when performed in an outpatient setting. The objective of this review was to evaluate all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated interventions aimed at reducing pain during hysteroscopic tubal sterilization. A comprehensive search was conducted between January and March 2011 across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, POPLINE, CENTRAL, EMBASE, LILACS, and CINAHL. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov, and reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed. Investigators were also contacted to identify any unpublished or additional studies. The inclusion criteria were limited to RCTs that assessed pain management during hysteroscopic sterilization, comparing interventions to either other interventions or placebo. Data extraction was initially performed by one reviewer and subsequently verified by a second reviewer. Analyses were conducted using RevMan software, and pain was measured using either a 10-cm or 100-point visual analog scale (VAS). When pain was assessed at multiple points during the procedure, the overall pain score was considered the primary outcome. If overall pain was not measured, a summation of pain scores across the procedure was used as the primary outcome. For continuous variables, the mean difference with a 95% confidence interval (CI) was calculated. Two trials met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 167 participants. In one trial, pain was measured using a 10-cm VAS. No significant difference in overall pain was observed between women who received a paracervical block with lidocaine and those who received normal saline (mean difference: -0.77; 95% CI: -2.67 to 1.13). Similarly, no significant differences in pain scores were noted during specific procedural steps, such as injection of the study solution into the anterior cervical lip (mean difference: -0.6; 95% CI: -1.3 to 0.1), placement of the device in the tubal ostia (mean difference: -0.60; 95% CI: -1.8 to 0.7), or post-procedure pain (mean difference: 0.2; 95% CI: -0.8 to 1.2). Procedure duration (mean difference: -0.2 minutes; 95% CI: -2.2 to 1.8 minutes) and successful bilateral device placement (odds ratio: 1.0; 95% CI: 0.19 to 5.28) were also not significantly different between groups. However, during certain procedural steps, such as placement of the tenaculum (mean difference: -2.03; 95% CI: -2.88 to -1.18), administration of the paracervical block (mean difference: -1.92; 95% CI: -2.84 to -1.00), and passage of the hysteroscope through the external (mean difference: -2.31; 95% CI: -3.30 to -1.32) and internal os (mean difference: -2.31; 95% CI: -3.39 to -1.23), the use of a paracervical block with lidocaine resulted in lower pain scores compared to normal saline. In another trial, pain was assessed using a 600-point scale derived from the summation of 100-point VAS scores across six procedural steps. No significant difference in overall pain was observed between women who received intravenous conscious sedation and those who received oral analgesia (mean difference: -23.00; 95% CI: -62.02 to 16.02). Additionally, no significant differences were noted during specific steps, such as speculum insertion (mean difference: 4.0; 95% CI: -4.0 to 12.0), cervical injection of lidocaine (mean difference: -1.8; 95% CI: -10.0 to 6.4), hysteroscope insertion (mean difference: -8.7; 95% CI: -19.7 to 2.3), placement of the first device (mean difference: -4.4; 95% CI: -15.8 to 7.0), or hysteroscope removal (mean difference: 0.9; 95% CI: -3.9 to 5.7). Procedure time (mean difference: -0.2 minutes; 95% CI: -2.0 to 1.6 minutes) and recovery time (mean difference: 3.6 minutes; 95% CI: -11.3 to 18.5 minutes) were also not significantly different between groups. However, women who received intravenous conscious sedation reported lower pain scores during the insertion of the second tubal device compared to those who received oral analgesia (mean difference: -12.60; 95% CI: -23.98 to -1.22). In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to definitively recommend an optimal analgesic or anesthetic approach for hysteroscopic sterilization. Paracervical block with lidocaine was associated with reduced pain during certain procedural steps compared to normal saline, but it did not significantly reduce overall pain scores. Similarly, intravenous conscious sedation resulted in lower pain scores during the insertion of the second tubal device but did not significantly impact overall pain scores. Further research is needed to establish effective pain management strategies for this procedure.
